facts.statement: The federal share of an SS4A grant may not exceed 80 percent; recipients contribute at least 20 percent, from non-federal sources unless a statute authorizes otherwise.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), section C.5, PDF page 13. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: The FY 2026 SS4A notice limits the federal share to 80 percent of total eligible project costs and requires a local match of at least 20 percent, generally from non-federal sources.
facts.excerpt: "The Federal share of an SS4A grant may not exceed 80 percent of total eligible SS4A project costs. Recipients are required to contribute a local matching share of no less than 20 percent of total eligible project costs." (NOFO p. 13)

facts.statement: The FY 2026 SS4A notice set the application deadline at 5:00 PM EDT on May 26, 2026; grants.gov shows the opportunity closed and listed no posted or forecasted SS4A opportunity on 2026-11-14.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), PDF page 3. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790 | Grants.gov opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01, Safe Streets and Roads for All Funding Opportunity (fetchOpportunity API record 361291). https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/361291 | Grants.gov search2 API, keyword SS4A and keyword Safe Streets and Roads for All, statuses forecasted and posted. https://api.grants.gov/v1/api/search2
facts.supports: The FY 2026 notice closed to applications at 5:00 PM EDT on May 26, 2026, and grants.gov listed no posted or forecasted SS4A opportunity on November 14, 2026, so no open round exists for this text.
facts.excerpt: "Planning and Demonstration Grant and Implementation Grant applications must be submitted by 5:00 PM (EDT) on May 26, 2026." (NOFO p. 3); grants.gov record: oppStatus "closed", closeDate 05/26/2026; search2 with statuses forecasted|posted returned no SS4A opportunity.

facts.statement: The FY 2026 notice gives an expected funding range of $100,000 to $5,000,000 for Planning and Demonstration Grants.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), PDF page 2. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: The notice expects Planning and Demonstration Grants of $100,000 to $5,000,000.
facts.excerpt: "$305,678,320 is available for Planning and Demonstration Grants ... Expected funding range: $100,000 to $5,000,000" (NOFO p. 2)

facts.statement: The FY 2026 notice expects a period of performance between 24 months and five years, not to exceed five years.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), section D.3, PDF page 16. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: The FY 2026 SS4A notice expects a period of performance between 24 months and five years and caps it at five years.
facts.excerpt: "The expected period of performance for Planning and Demonstration and Implementation Grant agreements is between 24 months and five years ... may not exceed five years." (NOFO p. 16)

facts.statement: Table 1 of the FY 2026 notice lists seven action plan components.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), Table 1, PDF pages 18-19. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: Its Table 1 lists the components a qualifying action plan includes: leadership commitment and goal setting, a planning structure, safety analysis, engagement and collaboration, policy and process changes, strategy and project selections, and progress and transparency.
facts.excerpt: Table 1: Action Plan Components: Leadership Commitment and Goal Setting; Planning Structure; Safety Analysis; Engagement and Collaboration; Policy and Process Changes; Strategy and Project Selections; Progress and Transparency (NOFO pp. 18-19)

facts.statement: The FY 2026 notice says the safety analysis should include all roadways in the jurisdiction without regard to ownership, to the extent practical.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), Table 1, PDF page 18. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: The notice states that the safety analysis should include all roadways within the jurisdiction, without regard to ownership, to the extent practical.
facts.excerpt: "To the extent practical, the analysis should include all roadways within the jurisdiction, without regard to ownership." (NOFO p. 18)

facts.statement: Table 1 of the FY 2026 notice describes the Engagement and Collaboration component.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), Table 1, PDF page 19. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: Table 1 of the FY 2026 SS4A notice calls for engagement with the public, stakeholders and partners, analysis of what that engagement yields, inclusion of overlapping jurisdictions, and coordination with other governmental plans.
facts.excerpt: "Robust engagement with the public and relevant stakeholders and partners ... Information received from engagement and collaboration is analyzed and incorporated into the Action Plan. Overlapping jurisdictions are included in the process. Plans and processes are coordinated and aligned with other governmental plans" (NOFO p. 19)

facts.statement: The FY 2026 notice defines Areas of Persistent Poverty and uses the same definition for Underserved Community.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), section B, PDF page 6. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790
facts.supports: The FY 2026 SS4A notice defines an Area of Persistent Poverty, and uses the same definition for an underserved community, as a county with 20 percent or more of its population in poverty over the 30 years before November 15, 2021, or a census tract with a poverty rate of at least 20 percent in the 2014–2018 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data.
facts.excerpt: "Any county that has consistently had greater than or equal to 20 percent of the population living in poverty during the 30-year period preceding November 15, 2021 ... Any census tract with a poverty rate of at least 20 percent as measured by the 2014 - 2018 5-year data series ... Underserved Community will use the same definition as APP" (NOFO p. 6)

facts.statement: Caltrans Standard Specifications 2023, section 82-3.04: a roadside sign on one post is one measurement unit of roadside sign - one post, and payment for furnishing sign panels is not included in the payment for roadside signs; section 82-2.04 pays for furnishing sign panels by area.
facts.source: California Department of Transportation, Standard Specifications 2023 Edition (unofficial version with vertical bars), sections 82-2.04 and 82-3.04 Payment, section 82-3.04, page 1111 of the unofficial version (PDF page 1115), and section 82-2.04. https://dot.ca.gov/-/media/dot-media/programs/design/documents/standard-specifications-2023-edition-unofficial-version-with-vertical-bars-dor.pdf
facts.supports: The sign count is a planning assumption, not a field inventory of curves, and the price covers that one bid item only: Caltrans pays for sign panels separately (2023 Standard Specifications, section 82-3.04), and traffic control, design and contingency are not counted.
facts.excerpt: 82-3.04: "An installed roadside sign consisting of one or more sign panels attached to: 1. 1 post is 1 measurement unit of roadside sign - one post" and "Payment for furnishing sign panels is not included in the payment for roadside signs."; 82-2.04: "The payment quantity for furnishing any type of sign panel is the area determined from the dimensions shown."

facts.statement: Entry 2438 applies to non-intersection crashes of severity K, A, B and C on rural, two-lane undivided roads with AADT of 261 to 14,790, from Washington data for 1993 to 2007, with no prior sign.
facts.source: CMF Clearinghouse, CMF / CRF Details, Countermeasure ID 2438, Install chevron signs on horizontal curves (FHWA, maintained by UNC Highway Safety Research Center), Applicability and Development Details. https://cmfclearinghouse.fhwa.dot.gov/detail.php?facid=2438
facts.supports: That factor applies to fatal and injury (KABC) non-intersection crashes on rural, two-lane undivided roads carrying 261 to 14,790 vehicles a day, studied in Washington State with 1993 to 2007 data, and it assumes no curve sign was there before.
facts.excerpt: "Crash Type: Non-intersection; Crash Severity: K (fatal),A (serious injury),B (minor injury),C (possible injury); Minimum Number of Lanes: 2; Maximum Number of Lanes: 2; Road Division Type: Undivided; Area Type: Rural; Traffic Volume: Minimum of 261 to Maximum of 14790 Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT); Date Range of Data Used: 1993 to 2007; State: WA"

project-overview.text:
This text is a demonstration prepared by an automated OpenPlan proof run from public sources read on November 14, 2026; the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe did not prepare, review, adopt or submit it, and it commits the Tribe to nothing.

The demonstration describes a Planning and Demonstration Grant request under the fiscal year (FY) 2026 Safe Streets and Roads for All (SS4A) notice to develop a comprehensive safety action plan for the public roads of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation in Nevada.

Section 24112 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act names a federally recognized Tribal government as an eligible entity, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs list published in the Federal Register on January 30, 2026 includes the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe of the Pyramid Lake Reservation, Nevada.

The 2020 Census counted 1,933 residents on the reservation, which the Census Bureau measures at 555.5 square miles of land and 174.0 square miles of water.

The Tribe's website gives the reservation's area as 475,000 acres or 742.2 square miles.

The Tribe's Strategic Transportation Safety Plan, dated December 2015, names State Routes 445, 446 and 447 on the reservation.

The FY 2026 notice closed to applications at 5:00 PM EDT on May 26, 2026, and grants.gov listed no posted or forecasted SS4A opportunity on November 14, 2026, so no open round exists for this text.

The attached safety action plan carries the crash summary, high-injury network, candidate countermeasures and benefit-cost summary the proof run produced.

safety-problem-and-impact.text:
The attached safety action plan reports and ranks the crashes the proof run retrieved.

Where the attached plan draws on the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), it holds fatal crashes only: NHTSA describes FARS as a census of fatal motor vehicle crashes on trafficways customarily open to the public, counting deaths within 30 days of the crash.

The Tribe's Strategic Transportation Safety Plan states that, according to Nevada Department of Transportation crash data for 2012 to 2014, the leading cause of crashes along the state routes was cited as ran off the road, and that the lack of shoulders along State Routes 445, 446 and 447 was highlighted as a safety concern (page 13).

This demonstration assumes two countermeasures from FHWA's Proven Safety Countermeasures list for up to three of the highest-ranked segments: Enhanced Delineation for Horizontal Curves and Lighting.

For the benefit estimate, this demonstration uses CMF Clearinghouse entry 2438, Install chevron signs on horizontal curves, with a crash modification factor of 0.84 and a four-star quality rating, from Srinivasan and others, Safety Evaluation of Improved Curve Delineation (2009).

OpenPlan's countermeasure list holds no crash modification factor for either countermeasure, and the attached plan says so beside each one; the factor used here is this demonstration's own reading of the CMF Clearinghouse.

That factor applies to fatal and injury (KABC) non-intersection crashes on rural, two-lane undivided roads carrying 261 to 14,790 vehicles a day, studied in Washington State with 1993 to 2007 data, and it assumes no curve sign was there before.

The benefit-cost analysis applies it to every death recorded on one treated segment, including any at an intersection or away from a curve, and assumes deaths fall by the same share the study found for all injury crashes combined; Lighting enters with no factor and no cost.

equity-and-underserved-communities.text:
The FY 2026 SS4A notice defines an Area of Persistent Poverty, and uses the same definition for an underserved community, as a county with 20 percent or more of its population in poverty over the 30 years before November 15, 2021, or a census tract with a poverty rate of at least 20 percent in the 2014–2018 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data.

For the reservation as a whole, the 2014–2018 ACS (table B17001) estimates 283 of 1,492 people for whom poverty status is determined, 19.0 percent, below the poverty level, with margins of error of 82 people for the count below poverty and 145 for the total.

The notice applies its 20 percent tests to counties and census tracts, not to reservations, and this demonstration did not test the counties or census tracts that cover the reservation.

The 2020 Census counted 1,117 of the reservation's 1,933 residents in rural territory and 816 in urban territory; this demonstration did not determine which Urban Area holds that urban territory, which the notice's rural test depends on.

How the action plan serves the people who use the reservation's roads, and which data it relies on, are decisions for the Tribe; this demonstration makes none of them.

engagement-and-collaboration.text:
No public engagement took place for this demonstration, and no one consulted the Tribe.

The two comments and the staff review summarized in Appendix E were entered by the automated proof run to test the comment, moderation and review screens; no resident, Tribal staff member or partner agency wrote them, and they are not evidence of opinion on the reservation.

Table 1 of the FY 2026 SS4A notice calls for engagement with the public, stakeholders and partners, analysis of what that engagement yields, inclusion of overlapping jurisdictions, and coordination with other governmental plans.

The Tribe's Strategic Transportation Safety Plan describes its own engagement: a public meeting with interactive display boards, a transportation safety survey, and a presentation to the Tribal Council (page 3).

Which partners to invite, and how and when to engage the community, are decisions for the Tribe; this demonstration makes none of them.

implementation-and-capacity.text:
Who manages the grant, who prepares the action plan, the schedule from award to adoption and the body that adopts the plan are decisions for the Tribe; this demonstration does not make them.

The Tribe's Transportation Planning web page states that its Transportation Planning Department dates from 2009 and that a program agreement entered in partnership with the Bureau of Indian Affairs lets the Tribe administer its own funds and work directly with FHWA.

The FY 2026 SS4A notice expects a period of performance between 24 months and five years and caps it at five years.

Its Table 1 lists the components a qualifying action plan includes: leadership commitment and goal setting, a planning structure, safety analysis, engagement and collaboration, policy and process changes, strategy and project selections, and progress and transparency.

The attached safety action plan covers part of the safety analysis component, fatal crash locations from the proof run's retrieval and a ranked high-injury network, and it supplies no leadership commitment, planning structure or policy review.

The notice states that the safety analysis should include all roadways within the jurisdiction, without regard to ownership, to the extent practical.

The Tribe's website posts a Strategic Transportation Safety Plan dated December 2015; whether it meets the notice's components is for the Tribe to determine.

This demonstration assumes chevron signs on one treated segment as an example item for the benefit-cost analysis; that choice is this demonstration's, not the Tribe's.

Enhanced Delineation for Horizontal Curves and Lighting both appear on FHWA's Proven Safety Countermeasures list page in its Internet Archive capture of November 4, 2026, read that way because FHWA's site refused automated reads on November 14, 2026.

FHWA's Lighting page states that research indicates continuous lighting on both rural and urban highways has an established safety benefit for motorized vehicles.

budget-narrative.text:
The budget amount, the match and its source are decisions for the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe; this demonstration sets none of them, and the attached budget document holds no cost estimate.

The FY 2026 SS4A notice limits the federal share to 80 percent of total eligible project costs and requires a local match of at least 20 percent, generally from non-federal sources.

For federally recognized Tribes, the notice states that Tribal Transportation Program and Tribal Transportation Program Safety Funds may be used as non-federal match, and it treats funding for Tribal lands as its own State under the 15 percent limit per State.

The notice expects Planning and Demonstration Grants of $100,000 to $5,000,000.

The one cost in this packet is the benefit-cost analysis's capital cost, which this demonstration assumes: 12 one-post roadside signs on one treated segment at $552.85 each, the weighted average unit price of 2025 awarded bids statewide for Caltrans item 820840, Roadside Sign - One Post, for a total of $6,634 in 2025 bid dollars.

This demonstration could not read a Nevada Department of Transportation unit price on November 14, 2026, so it uses the California price for a Nevada place.

The sign count is a planning assumption, not a field inventory of curves, and the price covers that one bid item only: Caltrans pays for sign panels separately (2023 Standard Specifications, section 82-3.04), and traffic control, design and contingency are not counted.

The analysis enters the cost as one outlay in its first analysis year, without escalation from 2025 dollars.

Set against one avoided death, that cost yields a very large ratio in the attached plan; the ratio rests on one segment, an assumed factor and an incomplete cost, and it does not show that the project is cost-effective.
